newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Osprey unveils global ambition.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Osprey unveils global ambition.

text.p: Singapore's Osprey Maritime Ltd said on Tuesday its US$750 million takeover of Monaco-based oil and gas carrier Gotaas-Larsen will make the group Asia's largest energy transportation group.

"The aim is growth and expansion of Osprey's activities. With the acquisition, Osprey will become a leading independent LNG operator in the international scene," chairman Tim Cottew told a news conference to announce the takeover.
Osprey will acquire 100 percent of Gotaas-Larsen Shipping Corporation, owned by Britain's reclusive Barclay brothers.

He said the purchase price was agreed after taking into account the open market value of the VLCCs, the future employment prospects of the LNG carriers and the expertise of the staff of Gotaas-Larsen.

He declined to say how much profit Gotaas-Larsen made last year but said the group "had not performed very well in the last few years" because its charters to Abu Dhabi ended. He refused to give details, saying the company was privately held.

The acquisition includes a total of nine vessels -- four liquefied natural gas (LNG) vessels, four very large crude carriers (VLCC) and a half-share in an LNG vessel which is already 50-percent owned by Osprey.
It will also take over six shipping-related companies with interests ranging from ship management to captive insurance.
Osprey was undertaking due diligence on Gotaas-Larsen and expected completion of the deal by July or August, Cottew said.

Osprey, majority owned by Indonesia's President Suharto's second son Bambang Trihatmodjo, owns and operates a fleet of 22 vessels transporting liquid cargo ranging from LNG to chemicals. After the acquisition, Osprey will own a fleet of 30 vessels and manage another six LNG carriers. Its total assets would amount to US$1.36 billion and it has more than US$600 million of committed future revenues.
"We are looking at growth. We will be able to field the best team in the industry for LNG and crude products," said Cottew.
He said the growth potential of the LNG market was particularly strong with Indonesia being the largest LNG exporter last year with 26 billion tonnes.
Cottew stressed Osprey's Indonesian origins and said the group has maintained very strong ties there. "We will use our history to continue to develop our ties there," he said.

He said three of the Gotaas-Larsen LNG carriers were under long-term charter and one was unemployed. With the group's emphasis on the LNG business, Osprey might consider selling two of the VLCCs, he added.

The takeover would be financed by net new debt of US$493 million from syndicated loan facilities and new equity of US$257 million. Gearing ratio for the company would remain at two times after the new issue of share, Cottew said.
He said the Barclays also believed in Osprey's prospects and, as part of the transaction, agreed to take a 20 percent stake in the joint company worth about US$60 million.
The new equity issues would result in Osprey doubling the number of shares available to the public and improve liquidity of the stock.
"The joint company should result in a rerating of our stock and also increase shareholder value," Cottew said.
